claim: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is a leading cause of death worldwide.
source: Cardiovascular disease (CVD), which ultimately damages heart muscle, is a leading cause of death worldwide (WHO, 2018).

claim: Myocardial infarction results in ischemia or lack of oxygen delivery to cardiomyocytes.
source: CVD encompasses a range of pathologies including myocardial infarction (MI), where ischemia or a lack of oxygen delivery to energy-demanding cardiomyocytes results in cellular stress, irreparable damage, and cell death.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about myocardial infarction pathophysiology

claim: GWAS have identified hundreds of loci associated with coronary artery disease.
source: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified hundreds of loci associated with coronary artery disease (Nikpay et al., 2015), MI, and heart failure (Shah et al., 2020), indicating the potential contribution of specific genetic variants to disease risk.
evidence: Supported by citations to Nikpay et al., 2015 and Shah et al., 2020

claim: Most disease-associated loci do not localize within coding regions of the genome.
source: Most disease-associated loci do not localize within coding regions of the genome, often making inference about the molecular mechanisms of disease challenging.

claim: Disease-associated variants are thought to have a role in regulating gene expression.
source: That said, because most GWAS loci fall within non-coding regions, these variants are thought to have a role in regulating gene expression.
evidence: Inference based on the non-coding location of GWAS variants

claim: The GTEx project has identified tens of thousands of expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs) across dozens of tissues.
source: The GTEx project has identified tens of thousands of expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs); namely, variants that are associated with changes in gene expression levels, across dozens of tissues including ventricular and atrial samples from the heart.
evidence: Supported by citation to GTEx Consortium et al., 2017

claim: eQTLs reported by GTEx explain a modest proportion of GWAS loci.
source: However, the eQTLs reported by GTEx explain a modest proportion of GWAS loci, and while increasing the diversity of tissues and sample sizes will enable further insight, orthogonal approaches also need to be considered.

claim: Many genetic variants not associated with gene expression at steady state may impact dynamic programs of gene expression in specific contexts.
source: It is becoming increasingly evident that many genetic variants that are not associated with gene expression levels at steady state, may be found to impact dynamic programs of gene expression in specific contexts.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies showing context-specific eQTLs

claim: Context-specific eQTLs have been identified in specific developmental stages.
source: This includes specific developmental stages (Cuomo et al., 2020; Strober et al., 2019), or specific exposure to an environmental stimulus such as endoplasmic reticulum stress (Dombroski et al., 2010), hormone treatment (Maranville et al., 2011), radiation-induced cell death (Smirnov et al., 2012), vitamin D exposure (Kariuki et al., 2016), drug-induced cardiotoxicity (Knowles et al., 2018), and response to infection (Alasoo et al., 2018; Barreiro et al., 2012; Çalışkan et al., 2015; Kim-Hellmuth et al., 2017; Manry et al., 2017; Nédélec et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies

claim: iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes have been shown to be a useful model for studying genetic effects on cardiovascular traits and diseases.
source: iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes (iPSC-CMs) have been shown to be a useful model for studying genetic effects on various cardiovascular traits and diseases, as well for studying gene regulation (Banovich et al., 2018; Benaglio et al., 2019; Brodehl et al., 2019; Burridge et al., 2016; de la Roche et al., 2019; Ma et al., 2018; McDermott-Roe et al., 2019; Panopoulos et al., 2017; Pavlovic et al., 2018; Ward and Gilad, 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies using iPSC-CMs

claim: Coronary artery disease can lead to myocardial infarction which results in ischemia.
source: In humans, coronary artery disease can lead to MI (Dzau et al., 2006) which results in ischemia and a lack of oxygen delivery to energy-demanding cardiomyocytes.
evidence: Supported by citation to Dzau et al., 2006

claim: Cardiomyocytes are unable to regenerate.
source: Given the inability of cardiomyocytes to regenerate, this cellular stress ultimately leads to tissue damage.

claim: A rapid increase in oxygen levels post-MI can generate reactive oxygen species leading to ischemia-reperfusion injury.
source: However, a rapid increase in oxygen levels post-MI can generate reactive oxygen species leading to ischemia-reperfusion (I/R) injury (Giordano, 2005).

claim: The study differentiated iPSC-CMs from iPSCs of 15 Yoruba individuals that were part of the HapMap project.
source: We differentiated iPSC-CMs from iPSCs of 15 Yoruba individuals that were part of the HapMap project (Banovich et al., 2018).

claim: The differentiation process was replicated three times from three individuals, yielding 21 differentiation experiments in total.
source: To obtain a measure of variance associated with the differentiation process, and to more effectively account for batch effects, we replicated the iPSC-CM differentiation from three individuals three times, yielding 21 differentiation experiments in total.

claim: The median cardiomyocyte purity on Day 30 was 81% (40–97% range).
source: On Day 30 (+/- 1 day), the median cardiomyocyte purity from one representative sub-culture across individuals was 81% (40–97% range), determined by flow cytometry as the proportion of cells that were positive for the cardiac-specific marker, TNNT2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Supplementary file 1; see Materials and methods).
evidence: Experimental data from flow cytometry measurements

claim: iPSC-CMs were first cultured at 10% oxygen for 7 days.
source: To do so, we first cultured the iPSC-CMs at oxygen levels that are close to physiological oxygen levels (10% oxygen - Condition A) for 7 days.

claim: iPSC-CMs were subjected to 6 hours of hypoxia at 1% oxygen.
source: We then subjected the iPSC-CMs to 6 hours of hypoxia (1% oxygen - Condition B), followed by re-oxygenation for 6 hours (10% oxygen - Condition C), or 24 hours (10% oxygen - Condition D) as previously described (Ward and Gilad, 2019).

claim: Oxygen levels were reproducibly controlled in cell culture.
source: Oxygen levels were reproducibly controlled in cell culture (Figure 1B, Supplementary file 1).

claim: Cytotoxicity levels increased following hypoxia and long-term re-oxygenation (p=0.01).
source: As expected, both cytotoxicity (p=0.01, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–B) and BNP (p=5×10−6, Figure 1—figure supplement 3C) levels increased following hypoxia and long-term re-oxygenation.
evidence: Experimental data from LDH activity assays

claim: BNP levels increased following hypoxia and long-term re-oxygenation (p=5×10−6).
source: As expected, both cytotoxicity (p=0.01, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–B) and BNP (p=5×10−6, Figure 1—figure supplement 3C) levels increased following hypoxia and long-term re-oxygenation.
evidence: Experimental data from BNP ELISA assays

claim: One sample (18852A) was excluded from analysis as a clear outlier.
source: We observed that one sample (18852A) was a clear outlier when comparing read counts for 18,226 autosomal genes across all samples, and thus excluded it from further analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Quality control analysis of RNA-seq data

claim: 12,347 expressed genes were analyzed after filtering.
source: We filtered out genes with low expression levels (see Materials and methods) to yield a final set with data from 12,347 expressed genes (see Materials and methods).

claim: Thousands of genes are differentially expressed between conditions at an FDR of 10%.
source: At an FDR of 10%, we identified thousands of genes that are differentially expressed between conditions (A vs. B = 4,983, B vs. C = 6,311; B vs. D = 6,792; A vs. D = 2,835; Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 6A).

claim: 2,113 genes (17% of all expressed genes) were classified as responding to hypoxia.
source: This approach led to the classification of 2,113 genes (17% of all expressed genes) as responding to hypoxia, which we term 'response genes' (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 6B–C), and 9,949 genes that do not change their expression level throughout the experiment which we term 'non-response genes'.

claim: Response genes are enriched for genes previously identified to respond to hypoxia in a Caucasian population (p<2.2×10−16).
source: Response genes are enriched for genes previously identified to respond to hypoxia in a Caucasian population of individuals (Chi-squared test; p<2.2×10−16; Ward and Gilad, 2019), and are highly enriched for gene ontologies in transcription-related processes (see Materials and methods, modified Fisher's exact test; p=1×10−19).

claim: Response genes are highly enriched for gene ontologies in transcription-related processes (p=1×10−19).
source: Response genes are enriched for genes previously identified to respond to hypoxia in a Caucasian population of individuals (Chi-squared test; p<2.2×10−16; Ward and Gilad, 2019), and are highly enriched for gene ontologies in transcription-related processes (see Materials and methods, modified Fisher's exact test; p=1×10−19).

claim: 1,573 genes with eQTLs (eGenes) were identified in at least one condition (q-value <0.1).
source: Using the combined haplotype test (CHT), an approach that leverages allele-specific information in small sample sizes (see Materials and methods; van de Geijn et al., 2015), we identified 1,886 SNPs which associate with gene expression (eSNPs) in at least one condition resulting in 1,573 genes with eQTLs (eGenes) in at least one condition (q-value <0.1; A: 613; B: 564; C: 564 and D: 464; Figure 3A–B; Supplementary file 2).

claim: 367 dynamic eQTLs were identified, classified as eQTLs in at least one, but not in all conditions.
source: This set of 367 dynamic eQTLs corresponds to 328 unique dynamic eGenes (see Materials and methods) and includes ZNF845 and RFC2 (Figure 3E) as well as PPARGC1, C8orf82 and CELF1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).

claim: The approach to classify dynamic eQTLs is associated with a false discovery rate of 48%.
source: Based on the p-value distributions of the corresponding eQTL associations in all other conditions, we estimate that our approach to classify dynamic eQTLs is associated with a false discovery rate of 48%.

claim: 32 of 326 dynamic eSNP-eGene pairs tested in GTEx are eQTLs in heart tissue (9.8%).
source: Thirty-two of 326 dynamic eSNP-eGene pairs tested in GTEx are eQTLs in heart tissue (9.8%), and 140 are eQTLs in at least one other assayed tissue (42.9%) demonstrating that many of these genes have context-dependent inter-individual variation in expression.

claim: Shared eSNPs are more likely to be eSNPs in heart tissue than dynamic eSNPs (p=0.01).
source: Shared eSNPs are therefore more likely to be eSNPs in heart tissue than dynamic eSNPs (Chi-squared test; p=0.01).
evidence: Statistical comparison of shared vs dynamic eSNPs

claim: Induced eGenes are significantly enriched for response genes (p=0.01).
source: However, we found a significant enrichment in response genes amongst induced eGenes (57 of 277 genes; Chi-squared test; p=0.01, Figure 3F) when compared to baseline eGenes, suggesting that induced eQTLs often impact the regulation of genes that respond to hypoxic stress.

claim: 327 of 1,639 annotated human transcription factors are response genes (p<2×10−16).
source: We found a significant enrichment of genes annotated as transcription factors amongst the genes responding to oxygen stress compared to non-response genes (327 of 1,639 annotated human TFs, chi-squared test; p<2×10−16; Figure 3F).

claim: Genes annotated as transcription factors are enriched in induced eGenes compared to baseline eGenes (p=0.004).
source: Indeed, genes annotated as transcription factors are enriched in induced eGenes compared to baseline eGenes (32 TFs; p=0.004), including MITF and PPARA, both of which are TFs that have been previously implicated in hypoxic response (Feige et al., 2011; Narravula and Colgan, 2001).

claim: 831 differentially accessible regions (DARs) were identified between hypoxia and short-term re-oxygenation.
source: Using a sensitive adaptive shrinkage-based approach with a False Sign Rate of 10% (Stephens, 2017), we could not detect changes in accessibility between baseline and hypoxia across 110,128 regions; however, we identified 831 differentially accessible regions (DARs) between hypoxia and short-term re-oxygenation (BC-DARs; 429 regions with increased accessibility and 402 with decreased accessibility), and 71 DARs between hypoxia and long-term re-oxygenation (BD-DARs; Figure 4A).

claim: There is a strong anti-correlation in effect size between normoxia-hypoxia and hypoxia-re-oxygenation conditions (Spearman correlation = −0.62; p=4.6×10−14).
source: Despite the fact that we do not identify any DARs between normoxia and hypoxia, there is a strong anti-correlation in the effect size between the normoxia (A) and hypoxia (B) conditions, and the hypoxia (B) and re-oxygenation (C) conditions across regions (Spearman correlation = −0.62; sign test p=4.6×10−14; Figure 4B) suggesting minor changes in accessibility in response to hypoxia that do not meet our significance threshold.

claim: DARs are more likely to overlap TSS than constitutively accessible regions (43% vs. 11%; p<2×10−16).
source: We found that DARs are more likely to overlap TSS than constitutively accessible regions (43% overlap vs. 11% overlap; chi-squared test, p<2×10−16; Figure 5A) suggesting that DARs may be involved in the gene regulatory response.
evidence: Statistical comparison of genomic feature overlap

claim: DARs are more likely to coincide with active histone marks in left ventricle heart tissue than constitutively accessible regions.
source: Indeed, DARs are more likely to coincide with active histone marks in left ventricle heart tissue than constitutively accessible regions (H3K4me3: 57% overlap DARs vs. 24% overlap constitutively accessible regions; chi-squared test; p<2.2×10−16; H3K4me1: 86% overlap DARs vs. 52% overlap constitutively accessible regions; p<2.2×10−16; Figure 5B).
evidence: Statistical comparison with ENCODE histone mark data

claim: HIF1α and HIF2α binding sites are more likely to overlap DARs than constitutively accessible regions (p=0.03).
source: We found that these HIF1α and HIF2α binding sites are more likely to overlap the 831 differentially accessible regions than the 109,275 constitutively accessible regions (Fisher test; p=0.03; Figure 5C).

claim: E2F4-bound regions are significantly enriched in DARs compared to constitutively accessible regions (p<2.2×10−16).
source: E2F4-bound regions are significantly enriched in DARs compared to constitutively accessible regions (Chi-squared test; p<2.2×10−16; Figure 5D).
evidence: Statistical comparison with E2F4 ChIP-seq data

claim: SINEs are specifically enriched in DARs (p=6.5×10−6).
source: We found that while three of the main TE classes, LINEs, LTRs, and DNA elements are similarly enriched in DARs compared to constitutively accessible regions; SINEs are specifically enriched in DARs (p=6.5×10−6; Figure 5E).
evidence: Statistical enrichment analysis of transposable elements

claim: CpG islands are enriched in DARs compared to constitutively accessible regions (p<2.2×10−16).
source: We found that CpG islands are enriched in DARs compared to constitutively accessible regions, whether these regions fall within 1 kb of TSS, which are typically enriched for CGIs, or not (p<2.2×10−16; Figure 5F).

claim: Response genes are more likely to have CGI promoters than non-response genes (p=0.002).
source: Indeed, we find that response genes are more likely to have CGI promoters than non-response genes (Chi-squared test; p=0.002).

claim: The median DNA methylation level is lower in DARs compared to all accessible regions (p<2.2×10−16).
source: While there is no difference in median DNA methylation levels between response and non-response genes, we found that the median DNA methylation level is lower in DARs compared to all accessible regions (p<2.2×10−16).
evidence: Statistical comparison of DNA methylation levels

claim: No differentially methylated CpGs were found across any pair of conditions when considering all 766,658 CpGs.
source: When considering all 766,658 CpGs we did not find any differentially methylated CpGs across any pair of conditions (10% FDR; Figure 6B), and all p-values are estimated to be true null p-values (pi0 = 1 when estimated by q-value across all pairs of conditions; Figure 6—figure supplement 3).

claim: Four differentially methylated CpGs were identified between baseline and long-term re-oxygenation when restricting to CpGs within CpG islands.
source: However, we identified four differentially methylated CpGs (DMCpGs) between the baseline (A) and long-term re-oxygenation condition (D; Figure 6C).
evidence: Statistical analysis of DNA methylation in CpG islands

claim: A lower proportion of variance is explained by 'condition' in DNA methylation data (0.8%) compared to gene expression data (6%).
source: We observed a lower proportion of variance explained by 'condition' in the DNA methylation data (0.8%) and chromatin accessibility data (3%) compared to the gene expression data (6%, t-test, p<2.2×10−16), and a corresponding increase in the residual variance (Figure 6—figure supplement 4).

claim: One induced dynamic eSNP (rs8053350) is associated with varicose veins.
source: By intersecting these two data sets, we found one induced dynamic eSNP (rs8053350) that is also associated with a measured phenotype in GWAS – varicose veins (Supplementary file 1; Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-B).

claim: Six dynamic eGenes are implicated in MI, heart failure, and stroke by GWAS gene mapping approaches.
source: Indeed, we found that six of our dynamic eGenes are implicated in these three disease states by GWAS gene mapping approaches (Supplementary file 1).

claim: The eSNP (rs12588981) for the dynamic eQTL EIF2B2 is nominally associated with CAD (p=4.7×10−5).
source: This set includes the eSNP (rs12588981) for the dynamic eQTL EIF2B2 which is nominally associated with CAD (GWAS association p=4.7×10−5) and is in high and statistically significant LD with the lead GWAS variant (GWAS association p=9.9×10−8) at this locus (rs3832966; R2 = 0.96, p<0.001; Figure 7; Figure 7—figure supplement 2).

claim: The eSNP (rs8105092) which regulates CARM1 in the hypoxic condition is nominally associated with MI (p=1.79×10−5).
source: We determined that eSNP (rs8105092), which regulates CARM1 in the hypoxic condition (condition B), is nominally associated with MI (GWAS association p=1.79×10−5) and in moderate, yet significant LD, with the lead GWAS variant (GWAS association p=2.8×10−9) at this locus (rs4804142; R2 = 0.32, p<0.001; Figure 7—figure supplement 3), and is not an eGene in LV or AA.

claim: Perturbation studies in relevant cell types can give insight into the molecular basis for genetic association with complex traits and disease.
source: These results suggest that perturbation studies in relevant cell types can give insight into the molecular basis for the genetic association with complex traits and disease, which might not be gleaned from the study of post-mortem tissues.
evidence: Inference from the integration of eQTL and GWAS data
